title: Dilucidationes super methodo elegantissima, qua illustris de la Grange usus est in integranda aequatione differentiali dx/√X = dy/√Y

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. E506 rewrites Lagrange's (Misc. Taur. IV) integration of Euler's equation dx/√X = dy/√Y. Lagrange introduces an auxiliary 'time' t so that the problem becomes a mechanical one, with dx/dt = √X and dy/dt = √Y. He then passes to p = x+y and q = x−y and finds a first integral of the resulting second-order system. That first integral is the algebraic integral of the separated equation.

Previous page (§§76–77). For X = B + Cx² + Dx⁴ + Ex⁶ (and Y the same in y), Euler obtains the algebraic integral
[B(x²+y²) + C(x⁴+y⁴) + Dx²y²(x²+y²) + 2Ex⁴y⁴ ∓ 2xy√(XY)] / (x²−y²)² = Δ.
With the initial condition y = 0, x = k this gives Δ = (B+Ck²)/k².

§78 (case B = 0). Now X = x²(C + Dx² + Ex⁴), so the equation becomes
dx/(x√(C+Dx²+Ex⁴)) ± dy/(y√(C+Dy²+Ey⁴)) = 0.
Under u = x² each term is du/(2u√(C+Du+Eu²)), so this is really an elementary (logarithmic/circular) addition law, not an elliptic one. The general integral keeps the same form with B = 0.

This page. The normalisation y = 0 → x = k now fails, because ∫dy/(y√...) diverges logarithmically at y = 0. Euler therefore fixes the constant by a general point: y = b corresponds to x = a. Substituting, with A = C + Da² + Ea⁴ and B = C + Db² + Eb⁴ (so that X(a) = a²A and Y(b) = b²B), gives
Δ = [C(a⁴+b⁴) + Da²b²(a²+b²) + 2Ea⁴b⁴ ∓ 2a²b²√(AB)] / (a²−b²)².

Conclusio §79. Euler claims his variant is simpler and easier to apply to all cases than Lagrange's own computation. Lagrange used dt/T and treated T as a function of p and q; Euler simply uses dt. He then says it is beyond doubt that this kind of analysis promises great growth. Yet it is not yet clear how to adapt it to integrations other than the cases treated here, which are the ones he had earlier derived from his 'canonical equation': the symmetric biquadratic relation of his earlier addition-theorem papers.
errors: The printed constant has ∓2ab√(AB). Since X(a) = a²(C+Da²+Ea⁴) = a²A and Y(b) = b²B, the term 2xy√(XY) at (a,b) equals 2a²b²√(AB). The correct formula is Δ = [C(a⁴+b⁴) + Da²b²(a²+b²) + 2Ea⁴b⁴ ∓ 2a²b²√(AB)]/(a²−b²)². Homogeneity confirms this: every other numerator term has degree 4 in a,b beyond the coefficients, while ab√(AB) has degree 2.
Notational clash: the letter B is redefined as C+Db²+Eb⁴ immediately after the coefficient B was set to 0. This is harmless but confusing.
Minor: Euler does not remark that the B = 0 case reduces, via u = x², to an elementary integral, so the 'notable case' is really a degenerate (logarithmic) addition law.

ideas.what: Fixing the integration constant of the algebraic integral by a general initial pair (a,b) when the base point y = 0 is a singularity (logarithmic divergence)
ideas.modern_name: Choice of base point for an addition theorem; avoiding a singular base point
ideas.where_published: E506 itself; similar normalisations in Euler's elliptic-integral papers (E251, E261 etc.)

ideas.what: Degenerate case B = 0: integral of dx/(x√(C+Dx²+Ex⁴)) ± dy/(y√(...)) = 0 in algebraic form
ideas.modern_name: Algebraic form of an elementary (logarithmic) addition law; degenerate elliptic case

ideas.what: Simplifying Lagrange's auxiliary-time method by using dt in place of dt/T
ideas.modern_name: Lagrange's mechanical/first-integral method for Euler's addition theorem (reparametrisation of time)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange 1766–69 (Misc. Taur. IV); Euler's simplification E506
ideas.where_published: E506; discussed in histories of elliptic integrals (e.g. Opera omnia I.21 introduction, unsure of exact pages)

ideas.what: Open question: how to extend the method beyond integrals derivable from the canonical biquadratic equation

missed.claim: Euler explicitly flags as open whether Lagrange's dynamical method extends beyond the elliptic cases arising from his canonical equation. This thread was resolved in other ways: Abel's theorem for the general case, and later the integrable-systems view of addition theorems. The question itself is well known to historians, so this is not genuinely missed.
missed.quote: tamen nondum patet, quemadmodum ad alias integrationes ea accommodari queat, praeter hos ipsos casus, quos hic tractauimus
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is an early statement of the problem of extending a mechanical (first-integral) derivation of addition laws to higher genus. That line was later pursued via Jacobi inversion and integrable systems, but it is already documented in the history of elliptic functions.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is the routine end of a known paper: a constant normalisation (with a printing or computation slip, 2ab√AB for 2a²b²√AB) and a concluding remark comparing Euler's method with Lagrange's. Lagrange's method and Euler's elucidation are standard in histories of elliptic integrals.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image, including the erroneous '∓ 2ab√AB'. Mathematically this should read ∓ 2aabb√(AB).
Footer: 'Acta Acad. Imp. Sc. Tom. II. P. I.' with signature 'H' and catchword 'DE'; correct as transcribed.
